name: Orthotropics

lead: Orthotropics is an approach to facial growth developed by British orthodontist John Mew, who held that resting tongue posture, mouth breathing and soft-food diets shape the jaws and face. Its popular offshoot is mewing, in which the tongue rests against the roof of the mouth, aimed at a more defined jaw and midface.

It is a major reference point in looksmaxxing communities. Proponents say the tongue, lips and jaws acting together influence how facial bones develop, and that malocclusion is largely environmental. Mainstream orthodontic bodies say evidence is inadequate, and a small study of 12 pairs of identical twins is among the few published comparisons.

paras: People practise tongue and lip posture and breathing habits daily, often starting in childhood or teens. Treatment in the approach can include palate expansion followed by a postural appliance (Mew's Biobloc system).

Posture exercises are widely discussed as low-risk, though forum users report jaw or joint discomfort. Mike Mew faced a misconduct process in the UK involving harm claims by child patients' families, and orthodontic appliances carry their usual risks.

angle.text: Followers of John Mew's orthotropics, the root of mewing, hold that tongue posture and oral habits shape the jaw and midface during growth, and adopt it for a more defined face. Mainstream orthodontic bodies say evidence for the facial effect is inadequate.

lead: Orthotropics is a theory and treatment approach founded by British orthodontist John Mew (1928 to 2025), which holds that the resting posture and function of the tongue, lips and jaws influence facial growth and that malocclusion is largely environmental [1]. Mew framed this as the 'tropic premise' in 1958 [1].

The approach has been popularised online as 'mewing', named by his son, orthodontist Mike Mew; media attention rose around 2019 [1][2]. Treatment can include palate expansion followed by a postural appliance, in Mew's Biobloc system [1].

Mainstream orthodontic organisations and reviewers say evidence for orthotropics is inadequate and that it is not a viable alternative to orthognathic surgery [1][2]. A small study of 12 pairs of identical twins treated with either orthotropics or fixed appliances is among the few published comparisons [3].
infobox: Tongue and oral posture shape facial growth

paras: According to Wikipedia, John Mew qualified in dentistry in 1953, trained in orthognathic surgery in 1956 and proposed the tropic premise in 1958. He visited Rolf Fraenkel in 1968 and, in 1987, won a High Court appeal against an NHS fine and helped found the International Association of Facial Growth Guidance [1].

Wikipedia reports that the General Dental Council reprimanded John Mew in 2010 over advertising it found misleading. It also reports that Mike Mew was expelled from the British Orthodontic Society and later faced regulatory action [1][2]. A 1992 paper by Mew argued that oral posture could influence middle ear function [4], and a 2014 British Dental Journal piece titled 'Orthotropics: will we never be free?' addressed the controversy [5].

Proponents say that a tongue resting on the palate supports the maxilla, and that mouth breathing and low tongue posture cause a recessed midface, narrow jaws and crooked teeth [6]. A looksmax.org guide describes this as 'craniofacial dystrophy' and lists mewing, intraoral face pulling and appliances as remedies [6].

A study published in 2007 compared facial changes in 12 pairs of identical twins treated 10 years earlier with either fixed appliances or orthotropic growth-guidance treatment without fixed appliances, using a panel of 12 lay judges [3]. It is a small study and the abstract describes the comparison rather than establishing a general effect.

A 1992 article proposed that tongue and oral posture might influence oropharyngeal development and middle ear aeration [4]. Wikipedia states that evidence for the efficacy of orthotropic treatment is inadequate [1][2].

Wikipedia reports that most orthodontists do not consider mewing a viable alternative to jaw surgery and that the American Association of Orthodontists has said there is no evidence it improves the jaw [2].
Orthotropics is discussed on looksmax.org as 'orthotropics/dontics', with long personal plans and recommended reading [7][8]. Some users report discomfort from mewing, such as jaw joint symptoms [6].

lore.intro: Orthotropics is the intellectual root of the mewing movement on looksmax.org, with users trading guides and treatment plans [7][6].
